summary: LUMINA is a web application that answers, in seconds, the question every lunar south pole mission must settle: if we land here, on this date, will the lander have sunlight for its solar panels and a line of sight to Earth? It draws the Sun and Earth over the real terrain horizon of any site, computed from NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) topography, and turns that geometry into sunlight, longest night, battery sizing, direct-to-Earth link and Deep Space Network contact windows. Sites and dates are compared side by side, and the tool proposes the best nearby landing spot and the best dates of the year. This matters because near the pole the Sun stays within about 1.5° of the horizon: our own results show that moving 40 m can halve the Earth link and a five-month launch slip can cut sunlight on a ridge from 100% to 56%. LUMINA lets mission planners, educators and the public see those trade-offs immediately.
details:
What it does. LUMINA evaluates a lunar landing site and date in under a second. For any of 37 cataloged sites (Artemis III candidate regions, CLPS, Apollo, Luna, Surveyor, ISRO, JAXA and CNSA landings, each with the source of its coordinates), a custom coordinate, or a click on the polar map, it shows:

A 360° panorama with the real terrain silhouette and the Sun and Earth drawn to scale, with a live countdown to sunset and Earthset.

Mission metrics: share of time with sunlight, longest night, share of time with an Earth link, outages, irradiance, panel power, daily energy, the minimum battery needed to survive the longest night, Earth eclipses, and a 0–100 viability index.

Contact windows with NASA’s Deep Space Network (Goldstone, Madrid, Canberra) and an optional antenna elevation margin of 2° or 5°.

Distance to the nearest permanently shadowed region, where water ice can survive, so science and engineering goals sit on the same screen.

A side-by-side comparison of sites and dates aligned by mission day, a 12-month calendar with the five best landing dates, and a search that maps the best landing spots within 2 to 10 km, excluding slopes above 15°.

A polar shadow map computed live on the GPU, a sunlit 3D globe, a first-person 3D view from the site at mast height, and animated playback of the whole mission.

A guided tour, a simple view, a glossary and plain-language verdicts in English and Spanish, plus CSV export, a one-page printed report and shareable links.

How it works. The browser computes the positions of the Sun and Earth and the orientation of the Moon (including libration) in a Moon-fixed frame with Astronomy Engine, in about 14 µs per instant. A Node.js server loads LOLA elevation models (nested 20, 40, 80 and 240 m grids at the south pole and a 474 m global grid) and casts 720 rays, one every 0.5° of azimuth, out to 400 km with lunar curvature, to obtain the true horizon of the site in about 55 ms. Because the Moon has no atmosphere, visibility is pure geometry: LUMINA measures what fraction of the Sun’s and Earth’s disks clears that horizon. Only the 720 horizon angles travel to the browser, which then recomputes the whole mission instantly for any date.

Validation. Sun and Earth directions agree with NASA/JPL Horizons (DE441) to within 0.0037° over 300 comparisons. At 2 m above the ground, computed sunlight matches published 20-year values: 82.1% against 82.0% and the same 165-hour longest shadow at Connecting Ridge (Gläser et al., 2018). Against NASA LOLA illumination maps, results fall within the published range in 10 of 11 sites. Where results differ (at ground level), we show it and explain why.

Benefits. When a launch slips or hardware changes, Artemis and CLPS teams can re-check alternative sites and dates in minutes instead of combining several specialist tools. Science teams (who want shadowed ice) and engineering teams (who need sunlight and a link) can negotiate with the same numbers. Educators and the public can see why the lunar south pole is so hard to explore.

What we hope to achieve. A fast, trustworthy first screen for landing site and date decisions. Next steps: 5 m topography around candidate sites, relay-satellite visibility for sites without line of sight to Earth, north pole terrain, launch-window constraints, and testing with mission planners and educators.

Tools and languages. TypeScript and JavaScript; React 19 and Vite for the interface; a custom WebGL2 shader and three.js for 2D and 3D graphics; Astronomy Engine for ephemerides; Node.js 22 and Express 5 with worker threads on the server; Vitest (257 automated tests) and Playwright (16 browser flows); GitHub Actions for continuous integration; deployed as a Node.js application on Hostinger. Version 1.0.0 was built in about 14 hours from 17 written specifications with measurable acceptance criteria.

Supporting material.

dataRefs: LOLA Gridded Data Records, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (NASA PDS Geosciences Node): polar elevation models LDEM_875S_20M, LDEM_85S_40M, LDEM_80S_80M and LDEM_75S_240M, and the global LDEM_64 (about 474 m). Used for every terrain horizon, the nearby-site search and the 3D terrain.

OLA polar illumination and permanent-shadow products (LPSR_75S_120M and the 60 m illumination maps; Mazarico et al., 2011). Used for the distance to permanently shadowed regions and to validate our sunlight and Earth visibility.
LROC WAC color mosaic (NASA Scientific Visualization Studio, CGI Moon Kit). Used to texture the 3D globe.

NASA/JPL Horizons System (DE441). Reference ephemerides used to validate our Sun and Earth positions and Moon elevation from the DSN stations, and queried live by the “Check with JPL Horizons” button.
NASA Artemis III candidate landing regions (press release, October 28, 2024), and landing coordinates published by NASA/LROC for Apollo 11, Apollo 17, IM-1 and IM-2.
